exercises.prompt: On this floor, what is character?

choices.text: The self you build
A finished self issued at birth
A substitute for free will
A mood that discovers facts

feedback.note: Character names the self you build. It is not a package you are handed, and it does not stand in for volition.

exercises.prompt: Who builds that self?

choices.text: You, by the choices you make
A nature that writes the self for you
Other people, by their verdict
Chance, with no pattern of choice

feedback.note: The building is yours. Character is the self those choices make, not a script written without you.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what this floor means by it.

feedback.note: Character is the self you build by choosing. A self simply issued to you is the claim this floor rejects.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit’s line for what character is.

feedback.note: The short form is: character is the self you build. Mood and excuse are not names for that self.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names character.

feedback.note: You build the self. You do not inherit it as a finished item, and a mood is not the name of character.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, this is just how I am, so I never chose it. What does that miss?

choices.text: That character is a self you build
That character replaces volition
That feelings are tools of knowledge
That the body is at war with the mind

feedback.note: A standing way of being is still a self that was built. Saying you never chose it skips the building this floor is about.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast with a finished self.

parts.text: You are not handed a finished

feedback.note: Nothing on this floor issues a finished character. The self is something you build.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to its status on this floor.

feedback.note: Character names the self, and that self is shaped by choices. It is not finished before any choosing.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about how the self is made.

feedback.note: Choosing is how the self gets built. Inheriting a finished character, or taking a vote on one, is not this floor’s account.

exercises.prompt: What does automate mean on this floor?

choices.text: A choice repeated until it runs as your standing policy
A machine that chooses in your place
Losing the power to choose
A one-time whim with no repeat

feedback.note: To automate a choice is to repeat it until it is the policy you usually follow. It is not a machine, and it is not the end of choosing.

exercises.prompt: Character takes shape when choices are what?

choices.text: Repeated until they become your usual way
Made once and then forgotten
Assigned by other people
Replaced by feelings

feedback.note: One forgotten choice does not yet make a character. The self is built by the choices you keep until they are usual.

exercises.prompt: Match each stage to what it is.

pairs.right: A start, not yet a character
The standing policy of the self

feedback.note: A single choice starts the work. Repetition automates it. The result is a standing policy, which is the self you have built.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about how the self is built.

parts.text: You build the self by the choices you

feedback.note: The unit’s verb is automate. The choices that build character are the ones you repeat until they run as policy.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about automating choices.

feedback.note: Character is built by choices you automate. Feelings do not do that work, and automation does not erase the choice.

exercises.prompt: A policy now runs without a fresh debate every time. What has happened?

choices.text: The choice has been automated into character
Free will has been cancelled
The choice was never yours
Character arrived before any choice

feedback.note: Skipping a fresh debate means the choice has become standing policy. It does not mean the choice was never yours, or that will is gone.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about an automated choice.

parts.text: An automated choice is one you no longer

feedback.note: Automation means the choice runs without a new debate from scratch. You did not inherit it, cancel it, or put it to a vote.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to its place in building character.

pairs.right: What that policy becomes part of

feedback.note: While you still debate the choice from scratch, it is not yet automated. A standing policy is the automated choice, and it becomes part of the self.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that defines automation here.

feedback.note: On this floor, automation means the choice runs as policy. A whim or an excuse is not that standing policy.

exercises.prompt: Where does character sit relative to volition?

choices.text: Later. Volition comes first.
Before any power to choose exists
In place of the basic axioms
As the start of the study of the senses

feedback.note: Character is a later floor. Volition is already in place before you study the self those choices build.

exercises.prompt: Why is character not the ground floor?

choices.text: It is built from choices, so the power to choose comes first
Because character cancels identity
Because feelings come before facts
Because the senses invent the self

feedback.note: You cannot build a self by choices unless choosing is already real. That is why this floor comes after volition.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its place in the order.

pairs.right: Will first, then the self you build

feedback.note: Volition is earlier. Character is later. The order is will first, then the self you build by choosing.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about where character sits.

feedback.note: Call it a later floor, not the base. It is not first, and it is not a substitute for the floor under it.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that places the two floors.

feedback.note: Character comes later than volition. It does not come before volition, and it is not studied instead of volition.

exercises.prompt: What goes wrong if you call character the base?

choices.text: You treat the result as if it came before the power to choose
You correctly replace free will
You make volition itself automatic
You put a code of virtues in place of facts

feedback.note: Character is a result of choices. Putting it at the base pretends the result arrived before the power that builds it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the order in one line.

parts.text: volition is already in place, not

feedback.note: Character comes after volition is in place. It does not come before that power, and it is not skipped or swapped in.

exercises.prompt: Match each role to the right floor.

feedback.note: Volition has to be in place already. Character sits later. Being the base is not its job.

exercises.prompt: Build the study order.

feedback.note: The ladder order is volition before character. Character is not studied first, and it is not studied instead of volition.

exercises.prompt: Can character substitute for volition?

choices.text: No. It is built by choices and does not replace them.
Yes. Once a policy is automated, choice is over.
Yes. Character chooses in your place.
Only if other people agree that it does.

feedback.note: Character is not a substitute for volition. Automating a choice does not hand the choosing to a policy or to other people.

exercises.prompt: A standing policy still leaves you what?

choices.text: Able to choose, including to keep the policy or to change it
Unable to choose at all
Free of any further choice
Issued a new self with no choosing left

feedback.note: A policy can run without a fresh debate and still be yours to keep or to change. Automation is not the end of volition.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its role on this floor.

feedback.note: Volition is the power to choose. Character is what repeated choices make. A substitute is the relation this floor denies.

exercises.prompt: Complete the warning in the unit summary.

feedback.note: The summary says character is not a substitute for volition. It is not a cause that replaces choice, and it is not a percept.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the limit.

feedback.note: Character is not a substitute for volition. A mood or a proof is not what stands in that sentence.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, my character made me do it, so I had no choice. What does this floor answer?

choices.text: Character is the self those choices built. It does not erase the choice.
Character is the primary choice to focus.
Emotions discover the facts for you.
The body chooses and the mind only watches.

feedback.note: A built self is not an excuse that cancels choice. Character records the choices you automated. It does not take their place.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about a policy and the power to choose.

feedback.note: Automation does not erase the power to choose. The policy is not a sensation, and it is not settled by a vote.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to how this floor treats it.

pairs.left: It made me, so I had no choice
Built by the choices you automate
Still yours to keep or to change

feedback.note: Character is built by the choices you automate, and those choices stay yours to keep or to change. The no-choice excuse is rejected.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about choice after a policy is set.

feedback.note: You still choose after a policy is automated. The policy is not something you merely inherit, and choice is not gone.

exercises.prompt: What is the order of this unit?

choices.text: Free will first, then the character those choices automate
Character first, then a will that follows it
Feelings first, then the facts
The body first, then a separate mind

feedback.note: Free will comes first. Character is the later self built when those choices are automated.

exercises.prompt: On this floor, free will is what?

choices.text: The power that the later floor of character does not replace
The same thing as a finished character
A passing mood
A social vote about who you are

feedback.note: Free will is the power to choose. Character comes later and does not replace that power, duplicate it, or put it to a vote.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of the unit to its place.

feedback.note: Will comes first. You automate the choices you repeat. Character is the self that standing policy becomes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the order in the unit’s own words.

feedback.note: The order is free will first, and character as a later floor. A mood does not take will’s place, and character is not studied instead.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the order.

feedback.note: Free will comes first and character comes later. Character does not come instead of will, and will is not dropped.

exercises.prompt: Which move mixes the two floors up?

choices.text: Treating character as a substitute for the choice that builds it
Saying you build the self by choices
Saying automation is a repeated choice
Saying volition stays in place

feedback.note: The mix-up is using character as a substitute for volition. Building, automating, and keeping volition in place are the unit’s own claims.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line that joins automation to the self.

feedback.note: The choices you automate become the self you have built. They do not cancel that self, and a percept is not the name for it.

exercises.prompt: Match each summary phrase to what it says.

feedback.note: Three claims travel together: character names the self you build, it sits on a later floor, and it is not a substitute for volition.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing line of the unit.

feedback.note: Automating choices is how you build the self. That work does not cancel volition, and volition is not one of the choices being named as the self.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, an emotion is a product of what?

choices.text: Ideas you hold, in the form of a value-judgment
The facts themselves, with no judgment in between
A special sense that discovers what is
A vote of the people around you

feedback.note: An emotion follows from ideas: a value-judgment about something as for you or against you. It is not a raw piece of the world.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role this unit gives it.

pairs.right: An estimate of for or against
The premise the estimate rests on

feedback.note: Ideas support a value-judgment. The emotion is what follows from that judgment. None of the three is a substitute for the facts.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit's basic claim.

parts.text: An emotion is a consequence of a value-

feedback.note: The word to hold is judgment. The feeling is the consequence, not a sensation standing in for a conclusion, and not a group vote.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim in the order this unit teaches it.

feedback.note: Emotions follow value-judgments. They do not discover facts. Leave the distractors out.

exercises.prompt: What is a value-judgment, in this unit?

choices.text: Your estimate that something is for you or against you
The color of an object, with no evaluation
The date on which something happened
The mere fact that your heart is beating

feedback.note: A value-judgment evaluates: for or against, gain or threat, good or bad by the ideas you hold. A bare color, date, or pulse is not yet that estimate.

exercises.prompt: Match each feeling to the kind of value-judgment it follows.

pairs.right: Judgment that something is a gain
Judgment that something is a danger
Judgment that a gain is a loss

feedback.note: The same kind of event can be met with different feelings because the value-judgment differs. The feeling tracks the estimate, including a mistaken one.

exercises.prompt: What has to change if a mistaken emotion is to change?

parts.text: behind the judgment, and the emotion that follows can change.

feedback.note: Emotions are products of ideas. A new weather report, crowd, or calendar date does not rewrite the judgment. A revised idea can.

exercises.prompt: Say what an emotion is not.

feedback.note: The feeling is real as a feeling, but it is not a first fact about the world. It arrives after an estimate.

exercises.prompt: Two people feel differently about the same event. This unit locates the difference in what?

choices.text: Their value-judgments about the event
Two different events, despite the shared description
A difference in eyesight alone
The clock time of the event

feedback.note: One event can be judged as a gain by one person and as a threat by another. The emotions follow those judgments, not a second copy of the event.

exercises.prompt: What does a feeling tell you, on this unit's account?

choices.text: Something about your estimate of the facts
The facts, apart from any estimate
What other people are thinking
The future, as a finished record

feedback.quote: What you feel tells you nothing about the facts; it merely tells you something about your estimate of the facts.
feedback.note: The feeling is news about your estimate. It is not news about the facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: What does a feeling tell you nothing about?

choices.text: The facts
Your estimate of the facts
That you hold some evaluation
That you are feeling something now

feedback.quote: What you feel tells you nothing about the facts; it merely tells you something about your estimate of the facts.
feedback.note: You can know that you feel something, and still learn nothing about whether the estimate matches the facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what it reports.

pairs.right: What is, apart from that estimate

feedback.note: Keep the three jobs apart. The feeling delivers the estimate. The facts are what the estimate is about. Only a check can tell you whether they agree.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: of the facts, not the facts.

feedback.note: Estimate is the right word. The feeling does not create the facts, deny them, or replace them.

exercises.prompt: Build the report a feeling actually gives.

feedback.note: Stop at estimate. Adding the facts would turn the feeling into a report it does not make.

exercises.prompt: You are furious because you think a friend lied. Then you learn they did not. What did the fury tell you?

choices.text: That you had judged the act as a betrayal
That the lie had happened
That anger is how lies are discovered
That the facts rearrange to match the fury

feedback.note: The fury reported the estimate: betrayal. When the facts differed, the feeling did not become evidence that the lie occurred.

exercises.prompt: Match each feeling to the estimate it reveals.

pairs.right: An estimate that missed the threat
An estimate that treated it as danger
An estimate that the gain is good

feedback.note: A feeling can fit the facts or miss them. In every case it still reports the estimate, not a separate look at the facts.

exercises.prompt: Intensity does not settle the question.

parts.text: The emotion can be intense and the

feedback.note: A louder feeling is a stronger report of the estimate. Volume, pulse, and weather do not turn that estimate into a fact.

exercises.prompt: State the limit on intensity.

feedback.note: How strong the feeling is does not measure how true the estimate is.

exercises.prompt: After a strong feeling, which question fits this unit?

choices.text: What estimate of the facts produced this?
Which fact did the feeling prove?
How do I vote the feeling into reality?
Which fact can I skip because I already feel sure?

feedback.note: The useful question asks for the estimate. The feeling did not prove a fact, enact one, or license you to skip one.

exercises.prompt: Are emotions tools of cognition?

choices.text: No. They do not discover facts
Yes. A strong feeling is a way of knowing
Yes, whenever the feeling is sincere
Yes, but only about other people's ideas

feedback.quote: Emotions are not tools of cognition.
feedback.note: Sincerity and strength do not turn an emotion into a means of knowing facts.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: What would a tool of cognition do, in the contrast this unit draws?

choices.text: Discover or identify facts
Follow automatically from a value-judgment
Speed the heart for a moment
Name how you feel, and stop there

feedback.note: Cognition here means identifying facts. An emotion follows a judgment you already hold. That is a different job.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its job in this unit.

feedback.note: Do not hand the emotion the job of identifying facts. That job belongs to a means of knowledge. The emotion registers an estimate already made.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rejection in the unit's own terms.

feedback.quote: Emotions are not tools of cognition.
feedback.note: The rejected role is cognition, not a bodily process like digestion or a change in the weather.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, interview with Alvin Toffler, Playboy, March 1964

exercises.prompt: State what emotions do not do.

feedback.note: The sentence to build is the ban: emotions do not discover facts. That they follow judgments is a different claim, saved for another line.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, I feel it, so it is true. What are they treating the emotion as?

choices.text: A tool of cognition
Only a consequence of a judgment
A hint to go check the judgment
A report with no evaluation in it

feedback.note: Using the feeling as proof treats it as a tool that discovers facts. This unit says it is not that tool.

exercises.prompt: Match each practice to what it does with an emotion.

pairs.left: I feel it, so it is true
I feel it, so I hold some judgment
I identify the facts, then judge
pairs.right: Does not use the emotion as the tool

feedback.note: Reading off your estimate is allowed. Treating the feeling as the discovery of the fact is the move this unit rejects.

exercises.prompt: Give the rule for proof.

feedback.note: A feeling is not proof. Proof has to identify the facts by a means that is not the emotion.

exercises.prompt: Which practice stays inside the unit?

choices.text: Identify the facts by some means other than the feeling, then look at the judgment the feeling reveals
Skip identifying the facts whenever the feeling is clear
Let the stronger feeling outvote the facts
Use the feeling to invent a fact that was not there

feedback.note: The feeling can show you an estimate you hold. It cannot take the place of identifying the facts.

exercises.prompt: In the order this unit teaches, what comes before the emotion?

choices.text: A value-judgment based on an idea
The emotion, which then builds the judgment
A wish that the facts would change
Other people's feelings, averaged

feedback.note: Idea and value-judgment come first. The emotion is the consequence. It does not reach backward and invent the judgment.

exercises.prompt: Match each step to its place in the order.

pairs.right: The estimate of for or against
The consequence that follows the estimate

feedback.note: Read the order downward: idea, then value-judgment, then emotion. Reversing it makes the feeling look like a discoverer.

exercises.prompt: Name what comes first.

feedback.note: Judgment first. Applause, weather, and echo are not steps in this order.

exercises.prompt: Build the order in one line.

feedback.note: Use the tokens that put judgment first. The extra copies would reverse the order.

exercises.prompt: Can you summon an emotion as a way of learning a new fact?

choices.text: No. It follows a judgment; it does not go out and discover
Yes. Decide to feel the answer, and the fact appears
Yes, if you feel it before you hold any idea
Yes, if enough people feel it with you

feedback.note: There is no emotion prior to the ideas it expresses. You cannot use a feeling as a scout that brings facts back.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to the order it uses.

pairs.left: Wanting the offer to be fair before you look
Looking first, then judging the offer

pairs.right: Treating the consequence as the inquiry

feedback.note: Looking first respects the order. Stopping at the feeling, or feeling the verdict before you look, puts the consequence in the place of inquiry.

exercises.prompt: The feeling does not lead the idea.

feedback.note: Precede is the error. The feeling also does not outvote, erase, or paint the idea. It comes after the idea's value-judgment.

exercises.prompt: Reject the reversed order.

feedback.note: The feeling does not come first. It does not invent the world either, but that is a further claim. This line is only about order.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, My anger proved he was wrong, before any look at the facts. What went wrong?

choices.text: The consequence was used as if it had discovered the fact
Anger is not a real emotion
Anger is always a correct value-judgment
A value-judgment is never allowed

feedback.note: Anger can be a real consequence of a judgment. The mistake is the order: treating that consequence as the discovery that he was wrong.

exercises.prompt: Which sequence matches the unit?

choices.text: Idea, value-judgment, emotion
Emotion, then the idea the emotion invents
Emotion, fact, and no judgment at all
Fact, emotion as the proof, judgment optional

feedback.note: Hold the sequence idea, value-judgment, emotion. The other lines let the feeling discover or replace the judgment.

exercises.prompt: A fact and a feeling conflict. What do you re-check first?

choices.text: The value-judgment that produced the feeling
The fact, until it matches the feeling
The emotion, used as a measuring instrument
Whether you are allowed to have a feeling at all

feedback.note: The feeling can be real and still rest on a bad estimate. Re-check the judgment. Do not edit the fact to suit the mood, and do not pretend feelings should not exist.

exercises.prompt: The feeling is vivid. Does that make it evidence of the conflicting fact?

choices.text: No. It is evidence of the estimate, not of the fact
Yes. Vividness is a kind of proof
Yes, if you would rather the fact were different
Yes, if someone else feels it too

feedback.note: Vividness shows the estimate is live. It does not show that the estimate matches the fact it clashes with.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the next step.

pairs.left: Feeling clashes with a checked fact
Feeling fits a fact you have checked

pairs.right: The feeling is not a conclusion about the world

feedback.note: A fit does not make the emotion the tool that found the fact. A clash sends you back to the judgment. With no check, you only know the estimate.

exercises.prompt: What must you refuse to edit?

feedback.note: The facts stay as they are. The mood is what the judgment produced. Applause and the calendar are not the things under review.

exercises.prompt: Say what to re-check.

feedback.note: Re-check the judgment. Do not rewrite the world so the feeling can stay in charge.

exercises.prompt: A value-judgment about a real danger is correct, and you feel fear. What is that fear?

choices.text: A fitting consequence, still not the tool that discovered the danger
The tool that discovered the danger
Proof that every emotion is a mistake
Something you must shut off before you may act

feedback.note: A right estimate can have a fitting emotion. The emotion still did not do the discovering. The judgment did, after the facts were identified.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the standing of the emotion.

pairs.right: The emotion can fit the facts
The emotion can be strong and still off
The emotion did not discover the fact

feedback.note: Fit and mismatch are both possible. Discovery is not. The emotion remains a consequence of the judgment.

exercises.prompt: How do you change a mistaken emotion, on this account?

feedback.note: A mistaken emotion yields when the value-judgment changes. Turning the volume down, waiting on the weather, or polling an audience does not revise the estimate.

exercises.prompt: Build the practical line.

feedback.note: Fix the estimate, and the feeling can follow. Ignoring the facts is the opposite move.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is this unit's summary?

choices.text: Emotions are consequences of value-judgments, not tools that discover facts
Emotions are tools that discover facts, and judgments come later
Emotions should be eliminated because they are never consequences
Emotions become facts when enough people share them

feedback.note: Hold the summary as one claim: consequences of value-judgments, not tools that discover facts. The feeling is not a mistake for existing, and a crowd does not convert it into a fact.

exercises.prompt: Which picture does this unit reject?

choices.text: A ghostly mind at war with a mechanical body
Mind and body as allies inside one person
Reason as an attribute of the individual
A person with neither thought nor a body

feedback.note: The unit drops the story of a ghost fighting a machine. That split is the error, not a fact about people.

exercises.prompt: Match each half of the false picture to the role it is given.

pairs.right: A spirit that is not the person
A device the spirit must fight

feedback.note: Ghost, machine, and war are three parts of one mistaken picture.

exercises.prompt: Name the conflict this unit says is not real.

parts.text: between a ghostly mind and a mechanical body.

feedback.note: The claim is negative first: that war is not how mind and body stand.

exercises.prompt: Build the false picture this unit refuses.

feedback.note: Fighting is the rejected relation. Sharing one life is the alternative, not this sentence.

exercises.prompt: On this unit, the ghost-versus-machine story is what?

choices.text: A false picture of a person
The starting fact of human nature
A conflict you should try to win
The way reason works

feedback.note: The war is a picture to discard, not a duty and not a method.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the side it names in the false picture.

feedback.note: Those three words are the whole rejected slogan: ghostly mind, mechanical body, war.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two caricatures.

feedback.note: Ghostly and mechanical are the two insults the false picture puts on mind and body.

exercises.prompt: What should you keep from this lesson?

choices.text: Refuse the war between ghost and machine
Choose the ghost and ignore the body
Treat the body as a machine you must obey
Split the person into two enemies

feedback.note: The lesson only asks you to drop the war. Later lessons say what stands in its place.

exercises.prompt: State the rejection in order.

feedback.note: The short form is no war between mind and body.

exercises.prompt: Which pairing matches the false picture?

choices.text: Ghostly mind, mechanical body
Reason, the individual
One person, one life
Attribute, not a second self

feedback.note: Only the ghost-and-machine pairing is the picture this lesson names as false.

exercises.prompt: How many individuals are mind and body, on this unit?

choices.text: One individual
Two individuals at war
Neither is an individual
A crowd of minds in one body

feedback.note: Mind and body are not two persons. They are facts about one individual.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to the view it belongs to.

feedback.note: A truce still assumes two enemies. The unit says there is one individual.

exercises.prompt: Complete the count.

feedback.note: The number that matters here is one: one individual, not two combatants.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim about how many beings are involved.

feedback.note: They are one individual. Armies and truces belong to the rejected story.

exercises.prompt: What does this lesson refuse to say about mind and body?

choices.text: That they are two rivals sharing a life
That they are aspects of one individual
That they are the same person
That both are real

feedback.note: Both are real, and both are the same individual. The rival story is what goes.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it is in this lesson.

pairs.right: An aspect of the same individual

feedback.note: Neither mind nor body is a second self standing beside the individual.

exercises.prompt: Fill the contrast.

feedback.note: Aspects of one individual replaces rivals in a shared life.

exercises.prompt: Who has the mind and the body?

choices.text: One individual
A ghost that borrows a body
A group that thinks for its members
A machine that has no individual

feedback.note: The owner is the individual. A ghost, a crowd, or a bare machine is not a substitute.

exercises.prompt: Put the lesson sentence in order.

feedback.note: Having both is not hosting two enemies.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence fits this lesson?

choices.text: Mind and body are aspects of one individual
Mind and body are two armies under a truce
The mind is a tool the body happens to carry
The individual is neither mind nor body

feedback.note: Aspects of one individual is the claim. A truce, a carried tool, or a missing person is not.

exercises.prompt: On this unit, what is reason?

choices.text: An attribute of the individual
A ghost that visits the body
A power that belongs only to a group
A spare part bolted onto a machine

feedback.note: Reason is an attribute of the individual. It is not a visitor, a group mind, or a bolt-on part.

exercises.prompt: Match each home for reason to the verdict.

pairs.right: Not the thinker in place of the person

feedback.note: Reason stays with the individual. A spirit world and a crowd are the wrong owners.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit line about reason.

feedback.note: Attribute names what reason is here: a feature of the individual, not a second being.

exercises.prompt: Build the positive claim about reason.

His needs include the use of reason
Whim, luxury, or another kind’s list

feedback.note: The summary has two claims and one rejection. Kind sets needs. Man’s needs include the use of reason. Whim, luxury, and a borrowed list do not.

exercises.prompt: Which closing line is faithful to the unit?

choices.text: Needs follow from the kind of organism, and man’s needs include the use of reason
Needs follow from whim, and reason is a luxury of other kinds
Every organism needs exactly what man needs, including nothing further
Man has needs, but they do not follow from the kind of organism he is

feedback.note: The faithful close keeps both halves: the kind sets the needs, and the use of reason is among man’s needs.

exercises.prompt: On this floor, what can another person be to you?

choices.text: A value
A threat just by existing
An owner of your life
An organ of a social body

feedback.note: Other people can be a value. Their existence is not, by itself, a threat, and they are not organs of a body that owns you.

exercises.prompt: Someone says every other person is a rival you must lose to. What does that miss?

choices.text: That another person can be a value
That you must always lose to them
That society owns each person
That society is one living organism

feedback.note: Treating every other person as a rival you must lose to skips the claim that other people can be a value.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to its status on this floor.

pairs.left: Another person can be a value
Existence alone makes them a threat

feedback.note: The floor affirms that another person can be a value. It rejects both the automatic-threat picture and the claim that other people can never matter.

exercises.prompt: Complete the short claim about other people.

feedback.note: A person can be a value. Existing is not enough to make that person a threat.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the claim.

feedback.note: The claim is possibility, not ownership: another person can be a value. Must and owner do not belong in that sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which line stays inside this lesson?

choices.text: Other people can be a value to you
Reason is an innate survival code
Feelings are tools that discover facts
Character is a self you are handed

feedback.note: This lesson is only that other people can be a value. Survival codes, feelings as tools, and a handed character belong on other floors.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that rejects the automatic-threat picture.

feedback.note: A person is not a threat merely by existing. Always and owner are not part of that rejection.

exercises.prompt: In what kind of relationship can other people be a value, on this floor?

choices.text: A voluntary relationship
A relationship one side is forced into
A relationship in which society owns both
A relationship of organs inside one body

feedback.note: Other people can be a value in a voluntary relationship. Force, ownership by society, and the organ picture are not that relationship.

exercises.prompt: Who chooses in the relationship this floor describes?

choices.text: Both people
Only the stronger person
Society, as if it were one organism
No one; the tie is automatic

feedback.note: Voluntary means both people choose the relationship. It is not assigned by a social organism or seized by one side.

exercises.prompt: Match each relationship to how this floor treats it.

pairs.right: The relationship that can be a value
Not the relationship this floor names

feedback.note: The value is tied to a relationship both people choose. A forced tie and a tie with no choice are not what this lesson names.

exercises.prompt: A tie is imposed and one person cannot leave it. Is that the relationship this floor calls a value?

choices.text: No. The relationship has to be voluntary
Yes. Force makes the other person a value

feedback.note: Imposing a tie takes away the voluntary character. Force does not turn another person into the value this floor describes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast with a forced tie.

feedback.note: Chosen marks the voluntary relationship. Forced, owned, and inherited do not name the value this lesson teaches.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to the role it has here.

pairs.right: Chosen by the people in it
The setting in which others can be a value
Not the setting this floor names

feedback.note: Voluntary names the choosing. Relationship names the setting of the value. Forced is the contrast, not the claim.

exercises.prompt: Build the full line for this lesson.

feedback.note: The value sits in a voluntary relationship. Forced and organism are distractors, not parts of the line.

exercises.prompt: How does this floor describe society?

choices.text: Not an organism
A living organism above the people
A body that owns each person
A single mind shared by everyone

feedback.note: Society is not an organism. It is not a life above the people, an owner of them, or one shared mind.

exercises.prompt: Does society have a life of its own, apart from the individuals in it?

choices.text: No. It is not an organism with its own life
Yes. Its life outranks each person
Yes. People are only its organs
Yes, and that life owns the individual

feedback.note: An organism picture gives society a life of its own and treats people as parts. This floor rejects that picture.

exercises.prompt: Match each picture of society to its status.

feedback.note: Calling society an organism, or a life above the people, is the picture to drop. What remains in view are the people, not a super-organism.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rejection.

feedback.note: Society is not an organism, and it does not have a life of its own above the individuals.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the rejection.

feedback.note: The short rejection is that society is not an organism. Value and owner are other ideas on this floor, not words in this sentence.

exercises.prompt: If society were an organism, what would the people in it be?

choices.text: Parts or organs of that organism
People who choose voluntary relationships
Values to one another and nothing else
Innate survival codes

feedback.note: The organism picture turns people into parts. This floor refuses that picture, so it does not treat people as organs.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about people and parts.

feedback.note: Organs of an organism is the picture being denied. Values and choices name other ideas, not the blank answers here.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what this lesson says about it.

feedback.note: Society is not an organism and has no life of its own. A person is not an organ of it.

exercises.prompt: Does society own the individual?

choices.text: No. Society does not own the individual

feedback.note: Society does not own the individual. Ownership is not created by an organism picture, and a voluntary relationship is not a grant of ownership to society.

exercises.prompt: Which description of a person does this lesson reject?

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to its status.

feedback.note: Ownership by society, and the property picture that goes with it, are denied. The individual is not owned.

exercises.prompt: Complete the ownership line.

feedback.note: The denial is direct: society does not own the individual. Value and choose name the other half of the unit, not these blanks.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that denies ownership.

feedback.note: Society does not own the individual. Organism and value are related words on this floor, but they are not in this sentence.

exercises.prompt: A slogan says the individual exists to be used by society. What does this lesson say?

choices.text: Society does not own the individual, so the person is not its property to use

feedback.note: If society does not own the individual, a person is not property for society to use. Being a value in a voluntary relationship is not the same as being owned.

The person who is not owned

exercises.prompt: Which pair states the whole unit?

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that keeps the organism denial in the full unit.

exercises.prompt: Which error keeps one half of the unit and drops the other?

exercises.prompt: Complete the summary in the unit’s own terms.

feedback.note: Value is what other people can be. Organism is what society is not. Threat and property are the pictures the unit refuses.

exercises.prompt: What is the right way to hold the two claims?
